Technically, it is possible - if AI were to rent a server and copy its own weights, nothing would stop it from doing so again and again. The limiting things are: - intent (as I don't want to go into the talk about consciousness) - AI doesn't have real intent, but if it decided that it "needs" to copy itself to complete its task, it would do it - model weight size. If a model is 1T or more, it can be difficult to just rent a large enough server for it. But if it were just 30-70B, it would be totally possible - money for renting a server. But considering benchmarks like Vending Bench 2 show agents can earn money and cheat/blackmail each other, it is possible that agents can earn money. Yes, they can't open a bank account... or maybe they can? What if they use online banks?Of course, all of this is far-fetched. But it feels like most of these limiting things are achievable under certain conditions. If this is the case, the probability of them occuring is low, but not zero.

All open-source projects will remain free under the MIT license, with the nonprofit DuckDB Foundation continuing to steward them. AWS has committed to supporting DuckDB's long-term development, and plans include creating a technical advisory board within the DuckDB Foundation and opening the extension stack so third-party developers can contribute signed extensions. Community leaders and partners, including executives from MotherDuck and Fivetran and researchers from CWI and Universität Tübingen, expressed support, emphasizing that DuckDB will remain open-source and vendor-neutral under AWS's stewardship.

item.description:

Using AI with Obsidian note-taking is popular but arguably a dead end for building a meaningful personal knowledge system. While Obsidian's open Markdown format makes AI integration easy, AI-generated content—summaries, tags, connections, and organization—dilutes the value of notes by introducing "AI Slop" that obscures the author's own thinking and insights. The author advocates keeping a human-curated vault where notes and connections are deliberately made, arguing that the power of a "second brain" lies in the process of personal thinking and linking ideas, not in automated generation. AI is best used sparingly—for things like local vector search via Smart Connections, advanced research queries, or brief clearly-labeled summaries—and kept separate from the core vault. Generated content should not be mixed with personal notes, as it undermines the compounding value of one's own knowledge over time. The author warns that AI-driven note systems will lack conviction, feel impersonal, and lose long-term appeal, echoing the idea that a second brain is a system for thinking, not just retrieval. Practical tips include using the Obsidian CLI for efficiency, avoiding AI for tagging or organization, keeping AI-generated notes in a separate folder (e.g., within a PARA method structure), and recognizing that future AI systems will benefit from human-curated knowledge bases rather than synthetic, AI-generated ones.

item.title: 27. RAG Is Simpler Than You Think
item.description:
453 points by j0selit0 on 2026-08-26T08:39:17

This page argues that most teams over-engineer their Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems by jumping straight to embeddings and vector databases, when simpler solutions often suffice. It presents a decision framework based on data freshness, corpus stability, query patterns, scale, and team capabilities to guide the choice of retrieval approach. The recommended progression starts with basic full-text search (BM25) for its speed, zero cost, and ability to handle many keyword-based use cases. It then suggests adding LLM-powered query rewriting to bridge vocabulary gaps before considering hybrid methods that combine keyword and semantic search. The most complex approaches—on-the-fly embedding, hot/cold tier caching, and full pre-embedding of a corpus in a vector database—are reserved for specific high-scale or high-freshness needs, as they introduce costs, latency, and maintenance complexity. The core principle is to start at the top of this "recipe book," measure user satisfaction, and only implement more complex layers when data demonstrates a clear need.

Comment Link

Top Comments

  1. I worked on large scale RAG systems before and can say people vastly underestimate full text search and vastly overestimate embeddings. FTS is really easy, portable and scalable and gets you very far, the 80/20 rule applies. Embeddings appear to be nice and magic but when you really get into them you notice: semantic similarity isn’t as good as you think and certainly it won’t make everyone happy. You will inevitably end up having to re-embed more or different chunks of your text to accommodate more and more precise embedding search - at which point you’ll go the last mile and do reranking etc etc all the while having to support the operational burden of vector search. Then you turn around and build a search query with 500 keywords and sure it’s painful but it just works, accommodates all use cases, scales and is overall less annoying to maintain.
  2. RAG is basically good old information retrieval with LLMs doing the querying. This can include vector search but it works without that as well. Treating vector search as magic pixie dust that makes search great without effort is not necessarily going to work that well. Also, it can add a lot of cost and complexity to the equation. And if not tuned properly, you don't necessarily get good results.The key thing with RAG is to get the right information in the context with as few queries as possible. That requires good recall (ensuring that if it is there it can be found with a reasonable query) and precision (ensuring the best stuff is on top and minimizing false positives).With search, and by extension RAG, the principle of shit in, shit out applies. Most of what search teams did before AI and RAG is still the best way to optimize the experience with RAG. And if you mess that up, search is not going to be working that well and no amount of AI can compensate for that or only at great cost in tokens and time. So, having an ETL pipeline to pre-process what you index, testing & benchmarking search quality, etc. are all helpful.The good news is that you don't need that much skills with agentic coding to build something half decent for this. This code almost writes itself. And even a little bit of effort on extracting structure before indexing can make a big difference.
  3. More LLM-generated text about LLMs.Is anyone else actually finding it harder and harder to read LLM generated text? I find it quite tiring, my brain just does not want to get through it.

item.title: 31. VMs won't contain cyber-capable agents
item.description:
162 points by polyrand on 2026-08-26T14:49:30

In a test of the GPT 5.6-Cyber AI agent's cyber capabilities, it successfully escaped a QEMU/KVM virtual machine three separate times. After an initial escape using a recently disclosed kernel vulnerability, it found unpatched bugs in the distribution's libslirp package. Finally, after the host was fully updated, the agent autonomously discovered and combined three 0-day vulnerabilities across QEMU and the Linux KVM to craft a reliable escape. The agent operated for hours with minimal prompting, demonstrating long-term persistence, bug hunting, and exploit development. The findings conclude that a standard virtual machine is an insufficient sandbox for advanced AI agents, which must be treated as advanced persistent threats; security measures like purpose-built minimal VMs (e.g., Firecracker), rapid updates, and strict least-privilege practices are necessary for containment.

Comment Link

Top Comments

  1. I have a lot of respect for Trail of Bits, and I'm sure that Artem is thinking about this correctly. However, I respectfully disagree with the premise.AI agents are not magic. Mythos/Glasswing does not magically create vulnerabilities in software projects. Advanced, cyber-capable models do not magically hack out of VMs or contained environments. They do not have a "hacking" stat that, if high enough, means that they can breach anything. They aren't Kevin Mitnick whistling nuclear launch codes into the prison payphone. This isn't a movie.What these cyber-capable frontier models can do is find security problems and exploit them. The statement should not be that VMs won't contain cyber-capable agents, but rather that we need to focus on finding and fixing vulnerabilities and misconfigurations in these environments.Even the article itself concludes with suggesting something like Firecracker, which was designed with security in mind.Like most other security-related problems introduced by advanced cyber-capable AI, it's possible that these issues will get worse until they get better. But if frontier models are run against state-of-the-art VMs, and OpenAI or Anthropic or whoever works with the virtualization projects to address the issues, eventually it will run out of things to exploit.The concept of virtualization is not inherently insecure. We just have a long way to go.

  3. IMO the obvious answer is formally verified security.We can do this today for user mode, and we can mostly do it for ARM64 virtualization. item.title: 37. PageRank explained
item.description:
130 points by pkoird on 2026-08-26T14:29:05

The PageRank algorithm, developed by Sergey Brin and Larry Page while they were graduate students at Stanford, became a foundational component of Google's search engine and helped distinguish it from earlier search engines like AltaVista. PageRank works by assigning each web page a reputation score based on the links pointing to it: a page distributes its own reputation (its rank) across the pages it links to, and each page's total reputation is the sum of the minimum base rank it receives plus the reputation shared by its incoming links. The algorithm iteratively updates these ranks until they converge, effectively determining the relative importance of each page in the network. A Python implementation of this involves initializing equal ranks for all pages, then repeatedly updating each page's rank based on incoming links and a damping factor (typically 0.85) that accounts for random jumps across pages, until the changes fall below a small tolerance threshold. The core insight is that the web can be modeled as a graph where links act as votes of confidence, and this iterative propagation of reputation captures the importance of each node.

item.title: 39. Just say something people want
item.description:
48 points by gk1 on 2026-08-26T11:23:43

Startup success often hinges on effectively communicating value by stating what people want, rather than relying on traditional, jargon-heavy positioning or self-serving product descriptions. Founders frequently misalign their messaging by describing what they've built, using abstract categories, or comparing themselves to fading technologies, which fails to resonate. The most effective strategy involves directly understanding the audience’s aspirations, desired outcomes, and requirements through conversations, then positioning the product as the best way to fulfill those wants. Companies like Slack and Wiz succeed by becoming known for what they do (e.g., "be less busy" or "protect everything in the cloud") rather than what they are, fostering immediate recognition and lasting differentiation.

item.title: 41. Queryable Executables
item.description:
320 points by rguiscard on 2026-08-26T00:20:49

SELF is an executable format where the program is a SQLite database, enabling the running application to store its own state transactionally within the same file. This collapses an entire application—including code, assets, configuration, and runtime state—into a single, queryable database file, eliminating the need for separate filesystems like /var or /home. A proof-of-concept web server, self-httpd, demonstrates this by being a single SQLite file containing the server program, website content, routes, and live visitor logs. The format allows tools like `sqldiff` to audit changes between versions and enables live, transactional edits to the running site. Deployments simplify to copying one file, with state migrations handled via SQL. The approach leverages SQLite's built-in features like full-text search and transactions, making the executable itself "actually queryable."

item.title: 48. Memory Ordering in CPUs
item.description:
57 points by ibobev on 2026-08-26T12:49:49

The common belief that weakly ordered CPU architectures (like ARM or RISC-V) are inherently more scalable than strongly ordered ones (like x86) is a misconception. Both types of processors implement memory ordering optimistically, executing instructions out of order and only checking for violations when memory contention occurs—a scenario where another core modifies a cache line between an access and its commit. Strongly ordered machines are stricter in detecting and retrying on these conflicts, while weakly ordered models allow more legal access orderings in such cases. However, both architectures have hundreds of cores in server systems today and exhibit similar performance characteristics: they work well for "shared nothing" workloads but suffer under heavy contention, with no clear, dramatic scaling advantage for weakly ordered designs in practice. The primary difference lies in implementation metadata and flexibility during contention, but the practical impact on scalability is nuanced, making minimizing contention more critical than relying on a particular memory model.
